summary: A broad encyclopedic overview of Israel covering its geography, climate, demographics, languages, economy, technology, infrastructure, foreign relations and defense. It also traces the history of the land from antiquity through Zionism, the British Mandate, the 1947 UN partition plan and statehood to later conflicts and peace agreements such as Camp David and Oslo.
one_line: Encyclopedic overview of the State of Israel's geography, population, economy, politics and history from ancient times through the Oslo peace process.
key_facts: Israel is officially the State of Israel, a sovereign state in Western Asia on the southeastern Mediterranean shore and the northern shore of the Gulf of Aqaba; Tel Aviv is its financial and technology center while Jerusalem is its self-designated capital, whose sovereignty is internationally unrecognized.
Israel's population was estimated in 2017 at 8,777,580, of whom 74.7% were Jewish, 20.8% Arab and 4.5% others; it is the world's only Jewish-majority state.
Israel's sovereign territory under the 1949 Armistice lines is about 20,770 square kilometers, while the total area under Israeli control including the West Bank is 27,799 square kilometers.
Israel joined the OECD in 2010, has the second-largest number of startup companies in the world after the United States, and the largest number of NASDAQ-listed companies outside North America.

On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 (II), recommending a Plan of Partition with Economic Union that would replace the British Mandate with an Arab State, a Jewish State and an internationally administered Jerusalem.
In 1978 and 1979 Menachem Begin and Anwar Sadat signed the Camp David Accords and the Israel–Egypt Peace Treaty, and Israel withdrew from the Sinai Peninsula captured in the 1967 Six-Day War.

In 1993 Shimon Peres for Israel and Mahmoud Abbas for the PLO signed the Oslo Accords, giving the Palestinian National Authority the right to govern parts of the West Bank and Gaza; Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated by a far-right-wing Jew in November 1995.
The 1994 Israel–Jordan Treaty of Peace made Jordan the second Arab country to normalize relations with Israel; Israel has diplomatic relations with 158 countries.

Israel is a technology leader in water: the Ashkelon SWRO plant, the largest in the world, was named 'Desalination Plant of the Year' in 2006, and desalination provided roughly 35% of drinking water by 2014.
Israel has two official languages, Hebrew and Arabic; more than one million Russian-speaking immigrants arrived between 1990 and 2004, and some 130,000 Ethiopian Jews live in Israel.
The Israeli population rose from 800,000 to two million between 1948 and 1958, and approximately 1,150,000 Jewish refugees relocated to Israel between 1948 and 1970.

Israel's defense spending fell from 24% of GDP in 1984 to 7.3% by 2006, the US is expected to provide $3.15 billion per year in military aid from 2013 to 2018, and Israel ranked 148th of 162 in the 2015 Global Peace Index.
Theodor Herzl is credited with founding political Zionism; he published Der Judenstaat in 1896 and presided over the first Zionist Congress the following year.
In 2013 a record 3.54 million tourists visited Israel, with the Western Wall the most popular site, visited by 68% of tourists.
